context.concept_name: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts

coverage.learning_objective: Design resource contracts: specify one resource's CRUD contract.

required_facts.statement: A URL path identifies a resource, and an HTTP method supplies the operation semantics rather than the path alone determining the action.
Model an item resource with a path parameter for its identifier and a collection resource without that item identifier.
Specify retrieval with GET, collection-specific creation processing with POST, target replacement with PUT and removal with DELETE, preserving each method's semantics.
A creation contract can use 201 with a Location identifying the created resource, while an absent item can use 404.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders API should make item identity and operation meaning clear. The URL identifies what the client is addressing; the HTTP method contributes what is requested.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A URL path identifies a resource, and an HTTP method supplies the operation semantics rather than the path alone determining the action.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Model an item resource with a path parameter for its identifier and a collection resource without that item identifier. Specify retrieval with GET, collection-specific creation processing with POST, target replacement with PUT and removal with DELETE, preserving each method's semantics. A creation contract can use 201 with a Location identifying the created resource, while an absent item can use 404.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Use /orders for the collection and /orders/{order_id} for an identified item. Read GET on the item as retrieval and PUT on that same item as target replacement; the path alone does not distinguish those operations. POST on the collection can express collection-specific creation processing, while DELETE on the item expresses removal. For a successful creation contract, 201 can be paired with a Location identifying the created item, such as /orders/42. For an absent item, the contract can use 404. Walk through the same identifier with several methods so that resource identity remains stable while requested semantics change. Designing the contract this way also lets you explain each operation without inventing an action word in the path as its sole source of meaning.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A path is not a complete operation definition. The method supplies semantics alongside resource identity.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Design resource contracts: specify one resource's CRUD contract.

practice_anchor.objective: Specify an orders resource's CRUD contract using annotated Python variables for resource paths, HTTP methods, response statuses and the created item's Location. Represent the contract without implementing request handling.
practice_anchor.success: The contract distinguishes /orders from /orders/{order_id}, assigns GET to retrieval, POST to collection creation processing, PUT to item replacement and DELETE to item removal, and records 201 with Location /orders/42 for creation and 404 for an absent item.

live_code.required_skill: Express resource identity and HTTP operation semantics as contract data using basic typed variable assignments.
allowed_syntax: Annotated variable assignments using str and int
String literals for resource paths, HTTP methods and Location values
Integer literals for HTTP response statuses

Use empty strings and zero as placeholders.

No request-handling implementation is required.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the orders collection and identified item visible as distinct resources. Annotate GET retrieval, POST collection creation processing, PUT item replacement and DELETE item removal, with 201 and Location /orders/42 for creation and 404 for an absent item.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Resource identity organizes operations.
Stay within the current objective: Design resource contracts. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

coverage.learning_objective: Register path operations: register one resource's routes.

required_facts.statement: Create a FastAPI instance and register a handler with @app.get("/path"), @app.post("/path"), @app.put("/path") or @app.delete("/path") for the intended method and path.
A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations.
Routes are evaluated in order, so declare a fixed path before a conflicting parameterized path to prevent the latter from capturing it.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A FastAPI service may retrieve and replace an order at the same path. Registration must distinguish their HTTP methods and also avoid ambiguous route ordering.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Create a FastAPI instance and register a handler with @app.get("/path"), @app.post("/path"), @app.put("/path") or @app.delete("/path") for the intended method and path.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations. Routes are evaluated in order, so declare a fixed path before a conflicting parameterized path to prevent the latter from capturing it.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Treat registration as a lookup the application will evaluate. In the fixed-versus-parameter example, the request path /orders/current can match the parameterized form if that conflicting form comes first. Writing the fixed declaration later does not make it automatically win. Reverse that problematic order so the fixed route is declared first. Separately, a GET and a PUT on the same item path remain different operations because method participates in registration. Combining these two observations prevents a misleading shortcut: route specificity alone does not explain all matching behavior, and path text alone does not identify an operation. Record method, path and ordering when reviewing the declarations.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Register retrieval with @app.get and replacement with @app.put on the intended item path. They are different operations even though their path text matches. Now compare /orders/current with /orders/{order_id}. The fixed current route should precede a conflicting parameterized route, because routes are evaluated in order and the parameterized route can capture that path. Trace a request by asking which method-and-path operation is registered, then which route matches first. This separates two concerns: distinct methods on the same path do not collapse into one operation, while conflicting paths require deliberate order. Read the registration list as behavior the application will evaluate, rather than assuming fixed paths are automatically preferred regardless of where they were declared.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not assume the framework always chooses a fixed route over an earlier conflicting parameterized route. Declaration order matters.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Register path operations: register one resource's routes.

context.concept_name: Validated environment-based configuration with fail-fast startup

coverage.learning_objective: Validate environment settings: define one environment's settings.

required_facts.statement: Subclass BaseSettings from pydantic_settings and declare typed fields to load and validate external configuration.
Construct Settings() to read environment variables and validate their types, with missing required settings or invalid values producing validation failures.
Use SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env") as model_config when a dotenv file should provide settings; environment variables take precedence over its values.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A deployment supplies configuration from outside the application. Treating those values as already trustworthy skips the point where missing or invalid settings should be detected.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Subclass BaseSettings from pydantic_settings and declare typed fields to load and validate external configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Construct Settings() to read environment variables and validate their types, with missing required settings or invalid values producing validation failures. Use SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env") as model_config when a dotenv file should provide settings; environment variables take precedence over its values.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Configuration construction is a useful point to stop invalid external input. For the exercise, use a required typed setting and compare three conditions: valid environment value, missing required value and invalid value. Only the valid condition satisfies construction. When a dotenv file is configured, add a fourth comparison in which the same key appears in both the file and the environment; the environment wins. This is a source-priority rule, not a reason to skip type validation. The service should not depend on the reader silently knowing how to repair an invalid deployment setting. State which source supplies it and what construction accepts.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Define a Settings class inheriting BaseSettings, with typed fields for the service's required configuration. Construct Settings() to read environment variables and validate them. Try one missing required setting and one value that cannot satisfy its declared type; both should fail validation rather than becoming unchecked application inputs. If a dotenv file is part of the setup, set model_config with SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env"). When the same setting is supplied in the environment and the dotenv file, the environment value takes precedence. For an exercise, put different synthetic values in those two places and identify which one construction should use. This makes configuration source, priority and validation visible instead of relying on whatever value a developer happened to see in a local file.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A dotenv value does not override an environment variable. Missing required configuration and invalid values are validation failures, not silent valid settings.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Validate environment settings: define one environment's settings.

segments.label: Declare typed settings and replace a default through the environment
segments.summary: A configuration module defines Settings by importing BaseSettings from pydantic_settings and subclassing it. The class declares app_name as a string with a default. Constructing Settings creates an object whose fields can be accessed by the application. The example first uses the default name, then supplies APP_NAME in the environment for a command. The resulting settings object uses that environment value instead of the default.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Configuration is external input validated at construction.
Stay within the current objective: Validate environment settings. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

coverage.learning_objective: Make managed async HTTP calls: use one reusable client with cleanup.

required_facts.statement: Use httpx.AsyncClient and await client.get(...), client.post(...) or another request method for an asynchronous outbound call.
Reuse a scoped AsyncClient instead of creating clients inside a hot loop to benefit from connection pooling.
Close a client with async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client or await client.aclose() at the end of its owning scope.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders handler needs data from an external service. The outbound call is asynchronous, but the client that owns connections also needs a clear lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use httpx.AsyncClient and await client.get(...), client.post(...) or another request method for an asynchronous outbound call.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Reuse a scoped AsyncClient instead of creating clients inside a hot loop to benefit from connection pooling. Close a client with async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client or await client.aclose() at the end of its owning scope.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: In the client-ownership drawing, several request arrows can pass through one client box. Connection pooling is the reason given for avoiding creation inside a hot loop. Closure belongs at the end of the owning scope, after that scope has finished using the client. The asynchronous request method and the asynchronous cleanup method have separate roles: awaiting get or post performs the call, while the context manager or aclose ends ownership. A request that has completed does not itself demonstrate that the client was closed. This is enough to explain the lifetime choice without adding a retry or timeout policy that this concept has not yet specified.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Use an httpx.AsyncClient for the outbound request and await its request method. Imagine several sequential lookups through the same owning scope: reusing that client lets the calls benefit from connection pooling rather than constructing another client inside a hot loop. At the end of the owning scope, close it using its async context manager or await client.aclose(). Trace ownership separately from each call: the scope creates the client, calls borrow it, and the scope closes it. That trace is useful whether the scope covers several operations or an application-lifetime resource. Keep the example focused on making and closing asynchronous requests; connection ownership does not by itself specify timeout policy or what a remote failure should mean to the local API.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An awaited request does not replace client cleanup. Reuse a scoped client where appropriate and close it at the end of that scope.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Make managed async HTTP calls: use one reusable client with cleanup.

The asynchronous call is placed inside an async function and executed. coverage.learning_objective: Validate domain invariants: add one custom invariant validator.

required_facts.statement: Use @model_validator(mode='after') on an instance method to check an invariant involving multiple already-validated fields.
An after-model validator raises ValueError when its invariant fails and returns self when validation succeeds.
Use @field_validator('field', mode='after') with a classmethod for a custom check on one validated field, returning the validated value when accepted.

Verify a cross-field rule with input that passes each individual field's validation but violates the model invariant, asserting that model construction raises ValidationError; also verify a consistent input is accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A booking order can have individually valid start and end values that form an invalid pair. A domain invariant checks the relationship after ordinary field validation.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use @model_validator(mode='after') on an instance method to check an invariant involving multiple already-validated fields.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: An after-model validator raises ValueError when its invariant fails and returns self when validation succeeds. Use @field_validator('field', mode='after') with a classmethod for a custom check on one validated field, returning the validated value when accepted. Verify a cross-field rule with input that passes each individual field's validation but violates the model invariant, asserting that model construction raises ValidationError; also verify a consistent input is accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For a hypothetical rule that end must be later than start, supply two values that each satisfy its field type but put end before start. An after-model validator sees the already-validated fields and raises ValueError for that invariant failure; model construction raises ValidationError. Supply a consistent pair next and return self from the successful validator. Compare this with a single-field custom check: an after-field validator uses a classmethod and returns the accepted validated value. Keep the two roles distinct. The pairwise rule is not adequately demonstrated by sending a value that already fails its own field type, because that would not isolate the cross-field invariant. Choose test data that passes the local field checks and fails only the relationship you are trying to teach.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A cross-field rule is not proved by an input that already fails individual field validation. Isolate the invariant with individually valid values.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Validate domain invariants: add one custom invariant validator.

segments.label: Check a password-confirmation invariant after field validation
segments.summary: A registration model contains email, password and confirmation fields. A model validator compares the two password fields after individual field validation. It receives self, giving it access to the model instance rather than just one value, and does not use the classmethod decorator used for field validators. Constructing the model with two different password strings produces a validation error reporting that the passwords do not match.

bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates a mismatch failure. The text also covers returning self on success, the complete single-field validator pattern, and verifying both rejection of individually valid but inconsistent inputs and acceptance of consistent inputs.

coverage.learning_objective: Raise expected HTTP failures: implement one HTTPException rejection.

required_facts.statement: Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.
HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge.
FastAPI's default HTTPException response contains the supplied detail under the JSON key detail.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An absent order is an expected API rejection, not a normal successful result containing an exception object. HTTPException expresses a deliberate HTTP outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge. FastAPI's default HTTPException response contains the supplied detail under the JSON key detail.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Read the expected-error branch as a change in control flow. Before the raise, the operation can execute its normal logic. At raise HTTPException, that normal path stops and the deliberate rejection is returned through the framework. Detail becomes the default response body value under detail, while supplied headers carry required metadata. A test should therefore inspect the declared status, detail structure and relevant headers rather than merely noticing an exception-shaped value. This mechanism expresses an expected HTTP outcome. It does not require exposing internal failures or returning the exception as an ordinary successful result.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: When the operation cannot find the requested order under its contract, raise HTTPException with the intended status and a client-facing detail. Raising stops the operation and produces the rejection; returning the exception object is not the same instruction. In FastAPI's default response shape, the supplied detail appears under the JSON key detail. If the rejection requires response metadata, provide headers on the exception, such as an authentication challenge when that outcome needs one. Trace the branch at which the exception is raised: normal operation work stops there, and the response is the deliberate HTTP rejection. Keep detail suitable for the client rather than using this mechanism as a reason to disclose internal diagnostic information.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Raise HTTPException rather than returning it. The default body puts the supplied information under detail, not under an arbitrary invented key.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Raise expected HTTP failures: implement one HTTPException rejection.

context.concept_name: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

coverage.learning_objective: Choose handler execution without blocking the event loop: choose and verify the handler execution mode for one I/O operation.

required_facts.statement: Use async def and await for an I/O library with awaitable operations; use a normal def handler for a blocking I/O library.
FastAPI runs a normal def path operation in an external thread pool, whereas an async def path operation runs as asynchronous execution.
FastAPI does not automatically move ordinary utility functions called directly by a handler to a thread pool; a blocking call inside async def can block the event loop.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A handler calls an I/O library. Choosing async def is only appropriate when the work can cooperate through awaitable operations; ordinary blocking calls do not become asynchronous because of the handler's spelling.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use async def and await for an I/O library with awaitable operations; use a normal def handler for a blocking I/O library.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI runs a normal def path operation in an external thread pool, whereas an async def path operation runs as asynchronous execution. FastAPI does not automatically move ordinary utility functions called directly by a handler to a thread pool; a blocking call inside async def can block the event loop.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare two hypothetical shipping clients: one offers awaitable I/O and the other offers blocking I/O. For the awaitable library, use async def and await its operations. For the blocking library, a normal def handler runs in FastAPI's external thread pool. Now move a blocking call into an ordinary helper called directly from an async def handler. FastAPI does not automatically move that helper to the thread pool, so the blocking call can block the event loop. Trace execution through the handler into the utility rather than inspecting only the route declaration. The decisive question is what boundary executes the I/O operation, not whether a helper has been placed in a separate file or given a name that sounds asynchronous.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI's handling of normal def path operations does not apply automatically to ordinary utility calls made directly inside an async handler.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Choose handler execution without blocking the event loop: choose and verify the handler execution mode for one I/O operation.

media.group_title: Handler execution and the event-loop boundary

segments.label: How FastAPI executes def and async def handlers
segments.summary: FastAPI automatically runs a normal def path operation in a separate thread pool, allowing the main event loop to continue processing other requests. An async def path operation runs on the event loop itself, where blocking I/O can stop other work from progressing. A normal def handler is therefore a valid execution choice, not inherently a wrong or slow one.

bridge_note.before: Watch for the execution boundary of each handler. Interpret the clip’s instruction to await I/O as applying to awaitable operations; adding await does not make a blocking library asynchronous.
bridge_note.after: The clip distinguishes handler execution modes but does not teach library-based selection or ordinary-helper dispatch. The text covers both: choose by I/O behavior, and trace directly called helpers within the handler’s execution boundary.

practice_anchor.objective: Choose the handler execution mode for a supplied blocking shipping-client operation, then verify the choice by tracing where the handler and its directly called utility execute.
practice_anchor.success: The path operation uses normal def, calls the supplied blocking operation without await, and returns its result. The execution trace places the handler and its direct utility call in FastAPI’s external thread pool rather than on the event loop.

live_code.required_skill: Select a handler declaration from the library’s I/O behavior and trace execution through a directly called utility.
allowed_syntax: await expressions for awaitable operations only
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide one shipping path operation with an editable declaration and an ordinary utility that directly calls the supplied blocking shipping client. Keep the route registration and client setup fixed, and state explicitly that the client operation is blocking.

coverage.learning_objective: Compose routers: assemble one service from feature routers.

required_facts.statement: Create an APIRouter for a feature's operations and register those operations on that router rather than requiring all handlers to live in the main module.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Order operations belong together, but the main application still needs to assemble them. APIRouter separates feature registration from application assembly.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Create an APIRouter for a feature's operations and register those operations on that router rather than requiring all handlers to live in the main module.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule

Keep those assembly choices visible at the include point rather than assuming they came from the feature's local path text. Follow the feature from router registration to inclusion so you can explain how it becomes part of the application. The router organizes operations; merely having the feature module present is not the assembly step.

context.concept_name: Typed path and query input binding

coverage.learning_objective: Declare typed URL inputs: declare one handler's URL inputs.

required_facts.statement: Put a name in the route path as {name} and declare name: Type in the handler to bind and convert that path value.
Handler parameters not present in the path are interpreted as query parameters when they are ordinary scalar types.
A query parameter with a default may be omitted, while a parameter without a default is required; the type controls conversion of a supplied string.
A path value that cannot be converted to its declared type produces a validation error instead of invoking the handler with that unconverted value.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A request for one order can also carry a query setting. FastAPI binds these values according to the path and parameter declarations rather than treating every input as the same source.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Put a name in the route path as {name} and declare name: Type in the handler to bind and convert that path value.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Handler parameters not present in the path are interpreted as query parameters when they are ordinary scalar types. A query parameter with a default may be omitted, while a parameter without a default is required; the type controls conversion of a supplied string. A path value that cannot be converted to its declared type produces a validation error instead of invoking the handler with that unconverted value.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Use one request to check each binding decision. The order identifier belongs to the path because the placeholder names it there. A scalar limit outside that placeholder is a query input, and its default decides whether omission is allowed. Supply a convertible identifier and then a nonconvertible one; the second should stop at validation rather than reach the handler as an arbitrary string. Separately omit the query input and compare its defaulted and required declarations. Keeping these comparisons separate shows that location, conversion and requiredness are independent parts of the declaration. A correct source binding does not by itself guarantee that every supplied value converts.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For /orders/{order_id}, declare order_id: int in the handler to bind and convert the path value. A scalar parameter named limit that is not in the path is a query parameter. If limit has a default, it may be omitted; without a default, it is required. Compare a supplied string that can convert to the declared type with an order_id that cannot: the invalid path value produces a validation error instead of reaching the handler as the original unconverted string. Draw one arrow from the path placeholder and another from the query string to their declared arguments. This keeps source binding, supplied-value conversion and omission behavior as three visible parts of the operation contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A parameter's name alone does not make it a path input. It must occur in the path declaration; ordinary scalar inputs outside the path bind from the query.

coverage.learning_objective: Serialize public responses: project one internal object.

required_facts.statement: Set response_model=PublicModel on the operation decorator to validate, serialize and filter the returned value to that public model.
Define the output model without private fields so those fields are not returned merely because they exist on the internal object.
When both a return annotation and response_model are supplied, response_model takes priority for FastAPI's response processing.
Returning a Response object directly bypasses automatic response-model conversion and filtering, so the application is responsible for that content.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An internal order object may contain fields the client must not receive. The public response model is an explicit output contract, not a request to serialize every available attribute.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Set response_model=PublicModel on the operation decorator to validate, serialize and filter the returned value to that public model.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define the output model without private fields so those fields are not returned merely because they exist on the internal object. When both a return annotation and response_model are supplied, response_model takes priority for FastAPI's response processing. Returning a Response object directly bypasses automatic response-model conversion and filtering, so the application is responsible for that content.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: For output review, start with the public model field list. Compare it with the internal object and identify a synthetic private field intentionally left out. Normal response-model processing filters to the public contract as well as validating and serializing. Then inspect the handler return form. A directly returned Response bypasses that automatic path, so the same field-list comparison does not establish that its content was filtered. This two-step review is more precise than saying "we have a response model, so all outputs are safe." Identify both the declared public schema and the actual response-processing boundary used by the operation.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Define a PublicOrder model containing only intended public fields, then set response_model=PublicOrder on the operation. Imagine the internal value also contains a private processing note: leaving that field out of the public model prevents it from being returned merely because it exists internally. Response processing validates, serializes and filters according to that public model. If the handler also has a return annotation, response_model takes priority for FastAPI's processing. Now compare returning a Response object directly: that bypasses automatic model conversion and filtering, so the application must take responsibility for its content. This is an important boundary to trace when checking disclosure: identify the return form, then identify which output-processing path it actually uses.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A response model is not an automatic safety net for a directly returned Response object. That path bypasses its conversion and filtering.

coverage.learning_objective: Inject service access with Depends: wire one endpoint to an authentication or database provider.

required_facts.statement: Declare a handler input with Annotated[Type, Depends(provider)] to have FastAPI execute the provider and supply its returned value.
Pass the provider callable to Depends rather than calling it in the declaration, so FastAPI can resolve its inputs.
A dependency makes a handler's needed input explicit and can be reused by multiple operations for shared input-provision logic.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Several order operations need a value supplied by reusable logic. A dependency makes that needed input part of the handler's declaration rather than an invisible global lookup.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a handler input with Annotated[Type, Depends(provider)] to have FastAPI execute the provider and supply its returned value.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Pass the provider callable to Depends rather than calling it in the declaration, so FastAPI can resolve its inputs. A dependency makes a handler's needed input explicit and can be reused by multiple operations for shared input-provision logic.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Read the provider declaration from the consumer backward. The handler needs an input of the declared type; Depends names the callable that supplies it. FastAPI can then resolve that callable inputs and execute it before giving the value to the handler. Passing provider rather than provider() keeps the callable available for that resolution. When another operation needs the same input-provision logic, it can declare the same provider. This makes reuse visible at each consumer rather than requiring the reader to discover an undeclared global. The declaration explains the needed input and its supplier; it does not itself claim the supplied value is stored for the whole application lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare an input as Annotated[Type, Depends(provider)]. Read that as an instruction for FastAPI to execute provider, resolve its inputs and supply its returned value to the handler. The declaration passes the provider callable, not the result of calling provider in advance. Trace the boundary in that order: provider definition, dependency declaration, request-time resolution, supplied handler argument. Another operation can declare the same provider for the same reusable input-provision logic. This makes the needed input visible where the handler is read. Keep attention on what the dependency supplies and how it is declared; this concept does not require treating all service logic as dependencies or inventing an application-wide hidden value store.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Depends(provider) passes a callable. Calling provider in the declaration would not express the same input-resolution instruction.

coverage.learning_objective: Bound the duration of an outbound HTTP call: configure and verify a finite timeout for one outbound operation.

required_facts.statement: HTTPX distinguishes connect, read, write and pool timeouts; read and write limits bound waiting for individual chunks rather than a whole request's elapsed duration.
Configure a finite timeout with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=seconds) or a request's timeout= argument; timeout=None disables timeout enforcement.
HTTPX raises timeout exceptions such as ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout and PoolTimeout when the corresponding wait exceeds its limit.

When the contract requires a total elapsed-time budget across asynchronous work, wrap the operation in async with asyncio.timeout(seconds); its cancellation is converted to TimeoutError outside the context.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An outbound lookup should not wait without a bound. But a chunk-level I/O timeout and a total elapsed-time budget answer different questions.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: HTTPX distinguishes connect, read, write and pool timeouts; read and write limits bound waiting for individual chunks rather than a whole request's elapsed duration.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Configure a finite timeout with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=seconds) or a request's timeout= argument; timeout=None disables timeout enforcement. HTTPX raises timeout exceptions such as ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout and PoolTimeout when the corresponding wait exceeds its limit. When the contract requires a total elapsed-time budget across asynchronous work, wrap the operation in async with asyncio.timeout(seconds); its cancellation is converted to TimeoutError outside the context.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For a hypothetical shipping lookup, configure a finite HTTPX timeout. Connect, read, write and pool waits have distinct limits, and read or write timeouts apply to waiting for individual chunks. A response that keeps supplying chunks within the read limit does not make that limit a whole-request elapsed deadline. If the local contract also requires the asynchronous work to finish within a total budget, wrap it in async with asyncio.timeout(seconds). Its cancellation is converted to TimeoutError outside that context. Compare a connection wait, a stalled response chunk and work exceeding the total elapsed budget, identifying the boundary for each. This separates the HTTPX timeout exceptions from the total-budget exception without assuming that one number attached to the client guarantees all elapsed work has the same bound.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: HTTPX read and write timeouts are not whole-request elapsed deadlines. Also, timeout=None disables timeout enforcement.

context.concept_name: Separating transport, testable business logic and persistence responsibilities

coverage.learning_objective: Separate service responsibilities: refactor one endpoint into boundaries.

required_facts.statement: A dependency can extract reusable input-provision logic from individual operation handlers and expose the supplied value as a declared handler parameter.

Transport handlers adapt HTTP inputs and outputs, business callables enforce application rules, and persistence adapters access stored state; separate these responsibilities so each can change without embedding the other responsibilities.

Move a business decision from a handler into a plain callable with explicit inputs, keep the HTTP adaptation in the handler, and call a separate persistence adapter for stored state rather than treating separate files alone as a responsibility boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A dependency can extract reusable input-provision logic from individual operation handlers and expose the supplied value as a declared handler parameter.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Transport handlers adapt HTTP inputs and outputs, business callables enforce application rules, and persistence adapters access stored state; separate these responsibilities so each can change without embedding the other responsibilities. Move a business decision from a handler into a plain callable with explicit inputs, keep the HTTP adaptation in the handler, and call a separate persistence adapter for stored state rather than treating separate files alone as a responsibility boundary.

context.concept_name: Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits

coverage.learning_objective: Choose suitable background work: choose one deferred operation's location.

required_facts.statement: Declare a BackgroundTasks handler parameter and call background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs) to schedule work after sending the response.
A background task callable can be a normal def or async def function; FastAPI handles either form.
BackgroundTasks work runs in the application process and cannot guarantee survival or delivery when that process fails.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operation can send its response before some small follow-up work runs. BackgroundTasks provides an in-process scheduling boundary, not a durable delivery guarantee.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a BackgroundTasks handler parameter and call background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs) to schedule work after sending the response.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A background task callable can be a normal def or async def function; FastAPI handles either form. BackgroundTasks work runs in the application process and cannot guarantee survival or delivery when that process fails.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a BackgroundTasks parameter and add a callable with background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs). In a hypothetical order workflow, the response is sent and then an in-process follow-up task runs. The callable can be normal def or async def; FastAPI handles either form. Trace a process failure after the response: the task is part of that process and its survival or delivery cannot be guaranteed. Therefore the response and the follow-up effect should not be described as if task scheduling proved durable completion. Keep this example to work whose contract fits that limitation. The important decision is not simply whether the follow-up is convenient to defer, but whether its required outcome is compatible with the process-local execution boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a background task does not prove that it survives process failure or delivers its effect. In-process scheduling is not durable completion.

live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an order handler, an order_id string, and a supplied small order_follow_up(order_id) callable. State that the follow-up is optional and losing it on process failure is acceptable. Leave its placement for the learner to complete.
live_code.observable_success: The handler declares background_tasks: BackgroundTasks and uses background_tasks.add_task(order_follow_up, order_id) before returning its response. It does not invoke order_follow_up directly or claim guaranteed completion.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an order handler registering follow-up work, sending its response, and then running the task inside the application-process boundary. Mark a process failure after the response as a point where pending work can be lost, separating response delivery from follow-up completion.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: In-process tasks cannot guarantee survival or delivery.

coverage.learning_objective: Compose subdependencies: compose one provider graph.

required_facts.statement: A provider can declare its own Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)] parameter, forming a dependency graph.
FastAPI resolves a provider's prerequisite inputs before calling that provider and supplies its result to the consuming operation.
A sub-dependency can declare typed query inputs of its own; those inputs are extracted from the request before its returned value is supplied to the dependent provider.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A handler may need a provider whose own result depends on another provider. Dependencies compose into a graph, so the prerequisites must be supplied before their consumer can run.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A provider can declare its own Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)] parameter, forming a dependency graph.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI resolves a provider's prerequisite inputs before calling that provider and supplies its result to the consuming operation. A sub-dependency can declare typed query inputs of its own; those inputs are extracted from the request before its returned value is supplied to the dependent provider.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an order-options provider depends on a pagination provider. The pagination provider declares typed query inputs and returns its result. FastAPI extracts those query inputs, resolves pagination, and supplies that value to order-options before calling it. Only then can the consuming operation receive the order-options result. Draw arrows from needed input toward the consumer, then trace execution from the request inputs through the prerequisite providers toward the handler. This avoids reading nested declarations as if the outer provider ran first and obtained prerequisites afterward. Each provider can expose its own needed inputs explicitly; composition is still input provisioning rather than a hidden sequence of global mutations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A provider does not run before its unresolved prerequisite inputs are available. Resolve the graph from prerequisites to consumers.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Compose subdependencies: compose one provider graph.

practice_anchor.objective: Compose a pagination provider, an order-options provider that depends on it, and a consuming path operation. Declare typed query inputs on the pagination provider and connect both dependency edges with Annotated and Depends.
practice_anchor.success: The pagination provider receives typed query inputs and returns a value consumed by order-options. The path operation receives the order-options result, with prerequisites resolved before their consumers.

live_code.required_skill: Declare nested provider dependencies and trace request inputs through prerequisites to the consuming operation.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide FastAPI and Annotated imports, an app instance, and incomplete pagination, order_options, and consuming-operation functions. Use only page and page_size as query-input names and returned dictionary keys.
live_code.observable_success: For a request carrying page=2 and page_size=10, pagination returns the typed values, order_options receives that dictionary through its declared dependency, and the consuming operation returns the order-options result. The completed declarations establish pagination before order_options before the operation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the dependency direction and execution order visible: typed page and page_size request inputs → pagination provider → order-options provider → consuming operation.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Prerequisites resolve before consumers.
Stay within the current objective: Compose subdependencies. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine provider execution order.

context.concept_name: Configuring existing middleware in the request/response stack

coverage.learning_objective: Configure existing middleware coherently: configure two maintained middleware components and trace their effects.

required_facts.statement: The last middleware added is the outermost wrapper: requests traverse it first, while responses traverse it last.
Configure each selected maintained middleware with app.add_middleware(MiddlewareClass, option=value), passing the component's documented options rather than writing its protocol implementation.
For two middleware additions, trace the request through the second addition then the first and into the handler, and trace the resulting response through the first addition then the second.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two maintained middleware components wrap a service. To reason about their order, picture nested wrappers rather than a flat list executed the same way in both directions.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: The last middleware added is the outermost wrapper: requests traverse it first, while responses traverse it last.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Configure each selected maintained middleware with app.add_middleware(MiddlewareClass, option=value), passing the component's documented options rather than writing its protocol implementation. For two middleware additions, trace the request through the second addition then the first and into the handler, and trace the resulting response through the first addition then the second.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Call the first addition A and the second addition B. B is the outermost wrapper because it was added last. The request travels B, then A, then the handler. The response travels back through A and finally B. Draw the handler inside A inside B and trace arrows inward and outward; the reversal becomes visible. Configure each component through app.add_middleware with its documented options rather than implementing its protocol yourself. When checking a supplied middleware stack, record addition order before tracing traversal. The same configuration list explains both directions, but the sequence differs because the response leaves the nested application boundary. A list labeled merely "middleware order" without a direction can obscure that distinction.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: The last addition sees requests first and responses last. Request traversal and response traversal are not identical sequences.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Configure existing middleware coherently: configure two maintained middleware components and trace their effects.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure supplied maintained middleware components A and B using their documented options, adding A first and B second. Annotate the request and response traversal through both components and the handler.
practice_anchor.success: Both components are configured with app.add_middleware and the supplied documented options. The annotations identify B as outermost, show requests traversing B → A → handler, and show the resulting response traversing A → B.

live_code.required_skill: Configure existing middleware through keyword options and trace the resulting nested application wrappers.
allowed_syntax: Keyword arguments using each supplied component's documented option names
live_code.starter_state_intent: Supply an existing app and handler, with A and B already bound to maintained middleware classes. Provide their documented option names and compatible values beside two empty configuration slots. No middleware implementation is required.
live_code.observable_success: The completed configuration adds A before B and passes documented keyword options to each. Comments correctly trace B → A → handler for the request and handler → A → B for the resulting response, without implementing either component.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the handler nested inside middleware A inside middleware B, label A as the first addition and B as the second, and draw separate request and response arrows in opposite directions.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Middleware wraps the application, so request and response traversal run in opposite directions.
Stay within the current objective: Configure existing middleware coherently. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Predict request and response traversal order of the configured stack.

context.concept_name: Production ASGI serving versus development reload

coverage.learning_objective: Choose production ASGI serving: run one production-appropriate command.

required_facts.statement: Run the application with an ASGI server import string, such as uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000, where main names the module and app names its application object.
--reload is useful during development but should not be enabled in production because it consumes resources and is less stable.
Uvicorn's --workers option starts multiple worker processes and is mutually exclusive with --reload; choose the worker count for the deployment rather than treating reload as process management.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A development server with automatic reload is convenient locally, but a production process needs deployment choices suited to stable serving.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Run the application with an ASGI server import string, such as uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000, where main names the module and app names its application object.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: --reload is useful during development but should not be enabled in production because it consumes resources and is less stable. Uvicorn's --workers option starts multiple worker processes and is mutually exclusive with --reload; choose the worker count for the deployment rather than treating reload as process management.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: In uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000, main names the module and app its application object. Verify that import string against the project structure. Leave --reload for development rather than enabling it in production. If the deployment chooses multiple worker processes, use --workers with the supplied worker count; it is mutually exclusive with --reload. Do not use reload as a substitute for that process choice.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Reload is not production process management. Worker count belongs to the deployment decision, and workers cannot be combined with reload.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Choose production ASGI serving: run one production-appropriate command.

practice_anchor.objective: Run uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 for the supplied application without development reload.
practice_anchor.success: The command starts the supplied application on the specified host and port without enabling reload.

live_code.required_skill: Use a module:application import string to start an ASGI application with Uvicorn and omit development-only reload.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an installed Uvicorn environment and an existing main.py module containing the application object app. Run from the directory containing main.py; no application edits are needed.
live_code.observable_success: Uvicorn imports main:app and starts serving on 0.0.0.0:8000. The executed command contains no --reload option; if a supplied worker count is used, it appears only through --workers.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the production command visible with main:app identified as module:application, the host and port options identified, and the absence of --reload apparent.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Production prioritizes stable process behavior.
Stay within the current objective: Choose production ASGI serving. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify development-only behavior.
